title: Radiant Floor Heating In Theory and Practice

findings.antecedent: Floor surface temperature change (5 K / 9°F)
findings.quote: a 5 K (9°F) change of the floor surface temperature will have the same effect as changing the air temperature by 2 K (3.6°F).

findings.antecedent: One degree change of floor temperature
findings.consequent: Effect on mean radiant temperature (and operative temperature)
findings.quote: one degree change of the floor temperature will have 2.5 times the effect on the mean radiant temperature (and operative temperature) than a change of the ceiling temperature.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating system
findings.consequent: Air temperature required for the same level of operative temperature
findings.quote: a floor heating system can reach the same level of operative temperature at a lower air temperature (Figure 15).

findings.antecedent: Radiant heating in buildings with high ventilation rates (e.g., industrial storage, hangars)
findings.quote: In buildings with high ventilation rates, such as industrial storage areas, hangars, etc., this has a significant influence on energy consumption and supports the use of radiant heating.

findings.antecedent: Increased insulation of buildings (walls/windows) and decreased heat loads
findings.consequent: Difference in performance between heating systems
findings.quote: By increasing insulation of buildings (walls/windows), and thus, decreasing heat loads, the difference between systems is less.

findings.antecedent: Floor temperature range of 19°C to 29°C (66°F to 84°F) in occupied zone for sedentary/standing occupants with shoes
findings.quote: a floor temperature range of 19°C to 29°C (66°F to 84°F) is recommended in the occupied zone for rooms with sedentary and/or standing occupants wearing normal shoes.

findings.antecedent: Maximum floor temperature for heating (29°C / 84°F) and minimum for cooling (19°C / 66°F)
findings.quote: For heating, the maximum temperature is 29°C (84°F), and for cooling, the minimum temperature is 19°C (66°F).

findings.antecedent: Design floor temperature of 35°C (95°F) outside the occupied zone (within 1 m from outside walls/windows)
findings.quote: In the European standard, it is acceptable to use 35°C (95°F) as the design floor temperature outside the occupied zone, i.e., within 1 m (3 ft) from outside walls/windows.

findings.antecedent: Occupants with bare feet (bathrooms, swimming pools, dressing rooms) and floor material
findings.quote: in spaces where occupants may have bare feet (bathrooms, swimming pools, dressing rooms), the optimal floor temperature for comfort also depends on the floor material.

findings.antecedent: Radiant floor heating
findings.consequent: Uniformity of temperature conditions from floor to ceiling (vertical air temperature differences)
findings.quote: One of the main features of radiant floor heating is the uniform temperature conditions from floor to ceiling.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating or large wall panel heater under window vs. more convective systems
findings.quote: Floor heating and the large wall panel heater under the window have a uniform temperature profile. The more convective systems have larger differences.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating
findings.consequent: Air temperature required to achieve 22°C (72°F) operative temperature
findings.quote: Figure 1 shows that the 22°C (72°F) operative temperature, using floor heating, was obtained at 1 K to 1.5 K (1.8°F to 2.7°F) lower air temperature than the other systems.

findings.antecedent: Increased stratification in high ceiling spaces (e.g., industrial workplaces, atriums, hangars)
findings.quote: In high ceiling spaces, such as industrial workplaces, atriums, and hangars, increased stratification significantly increases heat loss because of the increase in average space temperature.

findings.antecedent: Modern buildings with cold windows
findings.quote: there are seldom problems with radiant asymmetry from cold windows in modern buildings.

findings.antecedent: Air velocity lower than 0.18 m/s (36 fpm) at design conditions
findings.consequent: Necessity to compensate with heating below the window (to prevent draft)
findings.quote: If the air velocity is lower than the 0.18 m/s (36 fpm) at design conditions, it is unnecessary to compensate with heating below the window.

findings.antecedent: Radiant floor heating (allowing lower air temperature)
findings.quote: the air temperature can be kept lower than in “standard” houses. This has the advantage that the relative humidity in winter may be a little higher.

findings.antecedent: Lower air temperatures
findings.quote: studies show that people perceive air quality to be better at lower air temperatures.

findings.antecedent: Higher surface temperatures (from floor heating)
findings.consequent: Chance for condensation and mold growth / cold corners
findings.quote: Due to the higher surface temperatures, there is less chance for condensation and mold growth. Floor heating also prevents cold corners.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating
findings.consequent: Favorable living conditions for house dust mites
findings.quote: a study that shows that floor heating reduces the favorable living conditions for house dust mites compared to other heating systems.

findings.antecedent: Higher temperatures in carpets and mattresses
findings.quote: Higher temperatures in carpets and mattresses decrease the relative humidity.

findings.antecedent: Radiant heating systems vs. convective heating systems
findings.quote: Radiant heating systems result in less transportation of dust compared to convective heating systems.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating
findings.consequent: Need for cleaning heat emitters / carpets as pollutant source/sink / allergies
findings.quote: floor heating does not require cleaning heat emitters. Carpets are not as necessary when using floor heating, which eliminates a source for emitting pollutants and a sink source. This is especially helpful for people with allergies.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating system (29°C floor temperature, 20°C room temperature)
findings.consequent: Maximum heating capacity in the occupied zone
findings.quote: The maximum capacity in the occupied zone is about 100 W/m² (29°C [84°F]) floor temperature, 20°C (68°F) room temperature.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating system (35°C floor temperature, 20°C room temperature, within 1m from outside walls)
findings.consequent: Heat output / Average heat capacity (for a 4m deep room)
findings.quote: A 20°C (68°F) room temperature results in a heat output of 165 W/m². If the depth of a normal room is assumed to be 4 m (13 ft), the average heat capacity is 116 W/m².

findings.antecedent: Type of floor covering (tiles, wood, carpet)
findings.quote: This maximum heating capacity is independent of the type of floor covering (tiles, wood, carpet).

findings.antecedent: Thermal resistance of floor covering, system type, and pipe spacing
findings.consequent: Required water temperature to obtain maximum heating capacity
findings.quote: The required water temperature to obtain the maximum heating capacity is, however, dependent on the thermal resistance of the floor covering and other factors such as system type and pipe spacing.

findings.antecedent: Floor covering
findings.consequent: Required water temperature at different heating demands
findings.quote: Table 1 shows the influence of floor covering on the required water temperature at different heating demands.

findings.antecedent: Higher thermal resistance between pipes and floor surfaces
findings.quote: For other systems with higher thermal resistance between the pipes and floor surfaces even higher water temperatures are required.

findings.antecedent: Floor cooling system (26°C room temperature, 20°C floor temperature)
findings.quote: In most buildings a maximum cooling capacity at 26°C (78.8°F) room temperature and 20°C (68°F) floor temperature is then 42 W/m².

findings.antecedent: Direct sunlight on the floor (e.g., in atriums, airports, entrance halls)
findings.quote: Direct sunlight on the floor (as in atriums, airports, entrance halls) can cause the cooling capacity to be higher than 100 W/m2.

findings.antecedent: Including a separate pipe circuit at higher water temperature or shorter pipe spacing (<0.1 m)
findings.consequent: Surface temperature at the outside wall
findings.quote: A zone with a higher surface temperature at the outside wall is obtained by including a separate pipe circuit at higher water temperature or shorter pipe spacing (<0.1 m [0.3 ft]).

findings.antecedent: Water flow rate in a floor heating system
findings.consequent: Water temperature difference between supply and return
findings.quote: A water flow rate in a floor heating system often is based on a water temperature difference of 10 K (18°F) between supply and return.

findings.antecedent: Using a 5 K (9°F) temperature difference for the room with the highest load
findings.consequent: Average water temperature and heating capacity
findings.quote: For the room with the highest load, it is recommended to use only a 5 K (9°F) difference. This increases the average water temperature and then the heating capacity.

findings.antecedent: Shorter pipe circuits
findings.quote: To avoid pressure drops that are too high, the pipe circuits must be shorter.

findings.antecedent: Floor coverings with high thermal resistance (e.g., heavy wall-to-wall carpets)
findings.quote: For maximum capacity, it is important to avoid floor coverings with a high thermal resistance such as heavy wall-to-wall carpets.

findings.antecedent: Floor coverings with high thermal resistance
findings.consequent: Required water temperature and back losses to ground or unheated space
findings.quote: This increases the required water temperature and then also the back losses to ground or unheated space.

findings.antecedent: Higher water temperature
findings.consequent: Efficiency of the heat generator (condensing boiler, heat pump)
findings.quote: Also, higher water temperature reduces the efficiency of the heat generator (condensing boiler, heat pump).

findings.antecedent: Low heat loss in well-insulated buildings combined with changes in internal loads
findings.quote: The low heat loss in well-insulated buildings means that changes in internal loads have a higher impact on the room temperature than in buildings with standard insulation.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating systems (higher mass compared to other heating systems)
findings.consequent: Risk for overheating and additional heat loss
findings.quote: As floor heating systems often have a higher mass compared to other heating systems, it is often claimed that using floor heating means a greater risk for overheating and additional heat loss. However, several studies have found the opposite to be true.

findings.antecedent: Low-temperature heating system (e.g., floor heating) with very small temperature difference between room and heated floor
findings.quote: For a low-temperature heating system, such as floor heating, a significant effect is the so-called "self control" caused by the very small temperature difference between room and heated floor.

findings.antecedent: Small increase in room temperature
findings.consequent: Temperature difference between floor and space / Heat output from heated floor
findings.quote: A small increase in room temperature will significantly decrease the temperature difference between floor and space and then decrease the heat output from the heated floor.

findings.antecedent: 1 K (1.8°F) increase in room temperature
findings.quote: Table 1 shows the percentage decrease in the heat emitted from the floor by a 1 K (1.8°F) increase in the room temperature.

findings.antecedent: Well-insulated house (average heat load of 10 to 20 W/m² for heating season)
findings.quote: A well-insulated house has, on average, a heat load of 10 to 20 W/m² for the heating season. For these types of houses, the self-control effect corresponds to 30% to 90% (Table 1).

findings.antecedent: Standard floor heating systems with tubes embedded in concrete vs. low temperature radiator system (with controls)
findings.consequent: Room temperature control within acceptable limits
findings.quote: The results showed that, for both heating systems, the controls easily kept the room temperature within acceptable limits. There was no difference between the two systems.

findings.antecedent: Self-control mechanism
findings.consequent: Validity for electrically heated floor systems
findings.quote: This self-control is only valid for hydronic floor heating systems and not electrically heated floor systems.

findings.antecedent: Controlling the average water temperature (supply-return) instead of the supply temperature
findings.quote: Figure 4 show the advantage of controlling the average water temperature (supply-return) instead of the supply temperature.

findings.antecedent: Using an individual room control compared to a central control only
findings.quote: Figure 4 shows the energy advantage of using an individual room control.

findings.antecedent: Using an individual room control compared to a central control only
findings.quote: The studies showed a 15% to 30% energy savings by using an individual room control compared to a central control only.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating system vs. 100% convective heating system (warm air heating)
findings.quote: Compared to a 100% convective heating system (warm air heating), a floor heating system can reach the same level of operative temperature at a lower air temperature (Figure 15). This reduces ventilation heat loss compared to more convective heating systems.

findings.antecedent: Convective vs. radiant heating systems
findings.quote: The transmission heat loss is more related to the operative temperature and is more or less the same for convective and radiant systems.

findings.antecedent: Well-insulated buildings
findings.consequent: Need for efficient control for variations in internal loads (occupants, lighting, direct sunlight)
findings.quote: Well-insulated buildings require an efficient control for variations in internal loads from occupants, lighting and direct sunlight.

findings.antecedent: Self-control of floor heating systems combined with a room thermostat
findings.consequent: Efficient control for variations in internal loads in well-insulated buildings
findings.quote: The combination of the self-control of floor heating systems combined with a room thermostat makes an efficient control for variations in internal loads even in well-insulated buildings.

findings.antecedent: Floor heating (due to low water temperatures used)
findings.quote: Floor heating increases the efficiency of heat generators due to the low water temperatures used.
